cells.tense: The pen is in the hand here, and the bench work is steady.
cells.act: refine one distinction by close attention
cells.ask: Take one part of what's arriving and stay with only that — set it beside what's near it until you can say what makes it different. Everything else can wait.
cells.core:
What arrives has a shape you can work, and the work is narrow — one pass over the same ground, a little deeper than the last. You can tell the ripe from the raw, and an hour on the part only you can see is time well spent. Practice runs without strain, and time by yourself doesn't turn into distance from anyone. Once the distinction holds, the rest gets easier to carry.

So sharpen a single edge instead of sweeping the whole thing. Keep close attention on the difference that matters, and leave the backlog untouched. What you give up is the feeling of covering more ground. Refinement that serves the work rather than feeding a low hum of worry is what this balance is free to feed, and you get to choose which.
cells.sheetLine: The steady hand on the long work, one edge sharpened.
cells.verb: keeps a dedicated craft deepening through the long practice
cells.place: at the threshold where what's arriving first enters

cells.tense: The craft is being pushed toward a depth it hasn't reached.
cells.act: mark the good thing together, the day it happens
cells.ask: When something in the work comes through, say so that same day to the people who care about it — your own words — and stay a minute while they're glad with you.
cells.core:
Where the long practice lives, it gets driven further than it can yet go. Each pass has to be profound before it's finished, so what's still forming gets treated as if it has arrived. A good moment is filed before it gets its hour, and the next bench is set before this one is done. The pushing is real, and what's meant to grow the work has started to outrun the making.

Share what happens with the people close to the craft, on the day it happens, instead of pressing on with your head down. That gives up the privacy and the momentum. But a practice no one sees stays brittle, and those near you can't stay close to what they're not shown. Being glad alongside others doesn't slow the building — it keeps it from narrowing to one pair of hands.

cells.tense: The next attempt is being weighed before it has begun.
cells.act: put the frame on the table before anyone asks
cells.ask: When a person needs to know how something will go, state the order of it up front — what it is, and what comes first — before they ask. One plain sentence.
cells.core:
Something arrives, and its outline stays unspoken. A new practice, a new role, a new offer — and with nothing stated, the thing floats, and each person fills in the blank their own way. What's coming in gets met without a clear line around it. The knack for building something deep is yours to use. Here, it holds back.

Say the order of things once, plainly, before anyone asks. Not as a defence — just as the fact of it. That puts the frame back in your hands, and the ease it buys is worth more than the argument it might start. What arrives can be met with a clear structure, and direction can come from what you're genuinely engaged with.

cells.tense: The practice runs, and your telling has it running unattended.
cells.act: do the next piece at the speed you can keep for a month, not the speed you can keep for a day
cells.ask: Size the next piece of work to a pace you could hold for a month. If that's twenty minutes, do twenty, and close it there for today.
cells.core:
What's coming in gets carried because you hold a rhythm behind the scenes — the quiet hour, the same bench, the piece moving forward — and your own account leaves you out of it. You kept that rhythm going; the record of it is thin. You describe the work as running itself, and the people nearest you have not bought that. They don't have to.

Take the next piece at a pace you could hold a month, not a day, and stop while it's still easy. Twenty minutes, that size, then close it. That small stop puts the rhythm back under your hand and lets momentum stay even instead of surging and crashing. A week of it and the difference shows in how the work feels to pick up.
cells.sheetLine: The steady work runs because you keep the rhythm, not by itself.
cells.verb: keeps a dedicated craft deepening through the long practice
cells.place: at the threshold where what's arriving first enters

The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line implying the craft is already deep or the past is safely behind; I'll leave that out.
